--- title: "Types of models and learning" description: "Some models learn only the line between outcomes; others learn the data well enough to invent new examples. Some data come with answers; some do not. This page sorts machine learning along those two lines, with a short example of each on one coastal survey." order: 1 categories: [foundations, supervised, unsupervised] --- ## A map before the methods Machine learning comes with a long list of names: regression, classification, clustering, random forests, neural networks. They are easier to hold on to once you can place them on a map. This page draws that map with two divisions. The first separates models by the thing they learn. The second separates tasks by the data you have. ## One coastal survey runs through the course Every example in this course uses the same dataset: a survey of 800 stations on a temperate coastal shelf, visited between 2018 and 2023. At each station the survey measured the water and sampled the seabed, and counted one species of seabed animal. This page uses five of its columns: - **temperature**, the water temperature, in °C; - **salinity**, in practical salinity units (PSU), close to grams of salt per kilogram of seawater; - **depth**, in metres; - **abundance**, the number of animals counted at the station; - **present**, "yes" if at least one animal was found, "no" otherwise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() survey |> select(station_id, temperature_c, salinity_psu, depth_m, abundance, present) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station_id | temperature_c| salinity_psu| depth_m| abundance|present | |:----------|-------------:|------------:|-------:|---------:|:-------| |ST0001 | 11.15| 33.26| 99.2| 15|yes | |ST0002 | 4.42| 34.20| 134.7| 0|no | |ST0003 | 14.69| 33.67| 52.3| 0|no | |ST0004 | 10.02| 33.47| 90.8| 21|yes | |ST0005 | 6.35| 34.22| 125.0| 1|yes |
::: ::: The survey is simulated: we wrote the program that generated it, so we know the true relationships and can check whether a model finds them. It records more than these five columns, including chlorophyll, the type of seabed, the season and each station's position. [Section 2](../02-marine-data/index.qmd) introduces the full dataset and the work needed before modelling it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea ### Two things a model can learn Suppose the question is whether a seabed species is present at a station, given the water temperature there. A model can learn one of two things. A **discriminative model** learns the answer directly: the chance that the species is present, for each temperature. It draws the boundary between "present" and "absent" and nothing else. Most models in this course are discriminative, including linear and logistic regression. A **generative model** learns the data themselves. It describes the temperatures at stations where the species was found, and separately the temperatures where it was not. To classify a new station, it asks which of the two descriptions fits that station's temperature better. Because it has learned the data, it can also *generate* new ones: plausible temperatures for a station where the species occurs. The tools that write text or draw pictures are generative models of the same kind, on a vastly larger scale. ::: {.diagram} ![The same stations seen by two kinds of model. A discriminative model learns only the boundary between the groups; a generative model learns a description of each group, from which it can draw new examples.](img/discriminative-generative.svg){fig-alt="Two panels showing the same scatter of stations by temperature and depth: blue dots where the species was found, orange triangles where it was not. In the left panel, labelled discriminative, a dashed line separates the two groups. In the right panel, labelled generative, a shaded oval surrounds each group, and a hollow dot inside the blue oval is marked as a new example."} ::: Both can answer the same question. They differ in the thing they learn, and so in the assumptions they make and the extra jobs they can do. ### Two kinds of data The second division depends on the data you hold rather than the model you choose. **Supervised learning** learns from examples with a known answer. Each row has measurements and an outcome, such as a station with a recorded catch, and the model learns to get from one to the other. The outcome sets the task: *regression* for a quantity (how many animals), *classification* for a category (present or absent). **Unsupervised learning** has no outcome at all. It receives a table of measurements and looks for structure in it: groups of similar stations, or variables that move together. Nothing tells it which answer is right, so its results need extra care. A third kind, **reinforcement learning**, learns from the consequences of its own actions: an autonomous underwater vehicle might learn a sampling route by trial, rewarded for each useful measurement. It needs a way to act and a reward, not a table of data, and this course does not cover it. ::: {.diagram} ![Three kinds of learning. Supervised learning has an answer for every example; unsupervised learning has none and looks for groups; reinforcement learning acts, receives a reward, and adjusts. The table shows the first five stations of the survey.](img/learning-types.svg){fig-alt="Three panels. The supervised panel shows a table of five stations with columns for temperature, salinity and depth, and a highlighted answer column, found, reading yes, no, no, yes, yes. The unsupervised panel shows grey points by temperature and depth, falling into three dashed circles. The reinforcement panel shows a box for an underwater vehicle above a box for the sea, joined in a loop: an arrow labelled action, move and sample, runs down to the sea, and an arrow labelled reward and new position runs back up."} ::: ## Worked example Each idea above gets its own short example, followed by a comparison of each pair. Three quarters of the stations are kept for fitting and a quarter set aside for later pages. Three new stations, one shallow, one mid-depth and one deep, serve as the test case every model is asked about. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = present) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) new_stations <- tibble( station = c("shallow", "mid-depth", "deep"), temperature_c = c(12, 9, 5), salinity_psu = c(33.4, 33.7, 34.2), depth_m = c(40, 90, 150) ) ``` ::: These three stations are made up for illustration; they are not part of the survey. The names shallow, mid-depth and deep are labels we gave them from their depths (40, 90 and 150 m) so the text can refer to them. The models never see the names, only the three measurements. ### A discriminative model The question is whether the species is present, given the water temperature. The discriminative model here is **logistic regression**: linear regression adapted to a yes-or-no outcome, so that its answer is a probability between 0 and 1. A squared temperature term lets that probability rise and then fall again. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} discriminative <- logistic_reg() |> fit(present ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2), data = train) bind_cols(select(new_stations, station, temperature_c), predict(discriminative, new_stations, type = "prob")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:---------|-------------:|---------:|---------:| |shallow | 12| 0.8192281| 0.1807719| |mid-depth | 9| 0.8928872| 0.1071128| |deep | 5| 0.5837688| 0.4162312|
::: ::: For each new station it returns one thing: the chance of presence, and its complement. The species is likely at 9 °C and at 12 °C, and closer to a coin toss at 5 °C. That is all the model knows. ### A generative model The generative model answers the same question by learning the data instead. It describes the temperatures at stations with the species by a bell curve (a *Normal distribution*) with its own mean and spread, does the same for stations without the species, and records how common each group is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} generative <- train |> group_by(present) |> summarise(mean = mean(temperature_c), sd = sd(temperature_c), share = n() / nrow(train)) generative |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|present | mean| sd| share| |:-------|----:|----:|-----:| |yes | 8.95| 2.39| 0.78| |no | 8.11| 3.71| 0.22|
::: ::: The two groups have similar mean temperatures, but the stations without the species spread much more widely: the species is missing mainly from the coldest and the warmest water. To classify a new station, **Bayes' rule** weighs the two descriptions: how well each bell curve fits the station's temperature, times how common that group is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_present_generative <- function(temperature) { yes <- filter(generative, present == "yes") no <- filter(generative, present == "no") fit_yes <- yes$share * dnorm(temperature, yes$mean, yes$sd) fit_no <- no$share * dnorm(temperature, no$mean, no$sd) fit_yes / (fit_yes + fit_no) } new_stations |> mutate(.pred_yes = p_present_generative(temperature_c)) |> select(station, temperature_c, .pred_yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| |:---------|-------------:|---------:| |shallow | 12| 0.8035139| |mid-depth | 9| 0.8461345| |deep | 5| 0.6606586|
::: ::: Because it holds a description of the data, it can also generate new data. Here are five plausible temperatures for stations where the species lives, drawn from its bell curve: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} with(filter(generative, present == "yes"), round(rnorm(5, mean, sd), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 7.5 6.1 9.2 6.7 9.1 ``` ::: ::: ### Discriminative and generative compared @fig-two-models puts the two side by side. The left panel is the generative model's view: the data of each group, and the bell curve it fitted. The right panel shows the answer both models give, the chance of presence at every temperature. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} curves <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(2, 16, by = 0.1)) |> mutate( Discriminative = predict(discriminative, pick(temperature_c), type = "prob")$.pred_yes, Generative = p_present_generative(temperature_c) ) |> pivot_longer(-temperature_c, names_to = "model", values_to = "p") bell <- generative |> reframe(temperature_c = seq(0, 18, by = 0.1), density = dnorm(temperature_c, mean, sd), .by = present) |> mutate(group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")) observed <- train |> mutate(band = round(temperature_c)) |> summarise(p = mean(present == "yes"), stations = n(), .by = band) |> filter(stations >= 10) p_data <- ggplot(mutate(train, group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")), aes(temperature_c, fill = group)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1, alpha = 0.45, position = "identity", colour = NA) + geom_line(data = bell, aes(temperature_c, density, colour = group), linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Density", fill = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "The generative model learns the data") p_chance <- ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, p, colour = model)) + geom_point(data = observed, aes(band, p), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey55", size = 2) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("green", "purple")])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Chance the species is present", colour = NULL, title = "Both give a chance of presence") p_data + p_chance ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: the generative view, the temperatures at stations with and without the species, each summarised by a bell curve. Right: the chance of presence against temperature from both models, with the observed proportion in each one-degree band as points. The two models agree where most stations lie and part company at the edges.](types-of-learning_files/figure-html/fig-two-models-1.png){#fig-two-models fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel shows two histograms of temperature with a bell curve over each: stations with the species cluster between about 6 and 12 degrees, stations without it spread from about 3 to 15 degrees. The right panel shows two curves of the probability of presence against temperature, both rising from low values at 2 degrees to a peak near 0.85 to 0.9 around 9 degrees and falling again towards 16 degrees; the logistic curve falls more steeply at both ends. Points for the observed proportions follow the curves in the middle.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Discriminative | Generative | | --- | --- | --- | | Learns | The chance of presence at each temperature | The temperatures in each group, and how common each group is | | Answers "present or absent?" | Directly | Through Bayes' rule | | Can generate new stations | No | Yes | | Relies on | The shape of the probability curve | The shape of each group's data | Where most stations lie, between about 6 and 12 °C, the two agree closely. At the edges they part company, and the three new stations show it: at 5 °C the generative model is the more hopeful of the two. There the generative answer rests on its bell curves, and the stations without the species are not really bell-shaped: they sit at both ends of the range, not around a single middle. The discriminative model never had to describe them, so the wrong shape costs it nothing. ### Supervised learning Both presence models above were already supervised: every training station came with its answer, present or absent, so each was a *classification*. Here is one on all three variables: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classifier <- logistic_reg() |> fit(present ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:---------|---------:|---------:| |shallow | 0.8516393| 0.1483607| |mid-depth | 0.8928048| 0.1071952| |deep | 0.5163755| 0.4836245|
::: ::: Change the outcome to the number of animals counted and the same survey becomes a *regression* problem. An ordinary linear regression: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regression <- linear_reg() |> fit(abundance ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) tidy(regression) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------|----------:|----------:|----------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 21.6048715| 25.9757817| 0.8317313| 0.4058937| |temperature_c | -0.0838936| 0.0765104| -1.0964989| 0.2733033| |salinity_psu | -0.4286569| 0.7821813| -0.5480275| 0.5838782| |depth_m | -0.0282825| 0.0071275| -3.9680934| 0.0000813|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} bind_cols(select(new_stations, station), predict(regression, new_stations)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred| |:---------|--------:| |shallow | 5.149706| |mid-depth | 3.858663| |deep | 2.282957|
::: ::: Abundance falls with depth, by about 0.03 animals per metre. Salinity has no clear effect, which is correct: we built none into the simulation. The temperature slope is close to zero, even though the classification showed a strong link with temperature. [The next page](what-is-machine-learning.qmd) takes up that puzzle. ### Unsupervised learning Now remove the answers entirely: no abundance, no presence, only temperature, salinity and depth. We ask **k-means clustering** to sort the 800 stations into three groups. It works in four steps: 1. Place three group centres among the stations, at random. 2. Assign every station to its nearest centre. 3. Move each centre to the average of the stations assigned to it. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until no station changes group. "Nearest" is measured across all three variables at once, so they must be on a common scale first. Depth spans nearly 200 metres and salinity about two units; without rescaling, depth alone would decide every group. [Section 2](../02-marine-data/index.qmd) returns to this. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) clusters <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = 3) |> set_engine("stats")) |> fit(survey) clustered <- bind_cols(survey, extract_cluster_assignment(clusters)) clustered |> summarise( stations = n(), `depth (m)` = round(mean(depth_m)), `temp (°C)` = round(mean(temperature_c), 1), `salinity (PSU)` = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2), .by = .cluster ) |> arrange(`depth (m)`) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | stations| depth (m)| temp (°C)| salinity (PSU)| |:---------|--------:|---------:|---------:|--------------:| |Cluster_1 | 239| 45| 10.5| 33.35| |Cluster_3 | 298| 89| 9.2| 33.74| |Cluster_2 | 263| 133| 6.3| 34.07|
::: ::: The three groups follow depth: shallow and warm, mid-depth, and deep and cold. That is no surprise, because in this survey the three variables move together: salinity rises with depth, and temperature falls with it. The cluster numbers themselves mean nothing; k-means numbers its groups in whatever order it happens to find them. ### Supervised and unsupervised compared Ask both kinds of model about the three new stations. The supervised classifier gives a chance of presence; k-means gives a group. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_cols( select(new_stations, station), predict(classifier, new_stations, type = "prob") |> select(.pred_yes), predict(clusters, new_stations) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | .pred_yes|.pred_cluster | |:---------|---------:|:-------------| |shallow | 0.8516393|Cluster_1 | |mid-depth | 0.8928048|Cluster_3 | |deep | 0.5163755|Cluster_2 |
::: ::: The classifier's answer is about the species, because the species was its target. k-means returns only a number, `Cluster_1` to `Cluster_3`, which says nothing on its own. To give the groups names, the code below sorts them by the average depth of their stations, 45, 89 and 133 m in the table above, and calls them Shallow, Mid-depth and Deep. The names are ours; k-means knows only the numbers. With names attached, the groups can be compared with something k-means never saw: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Name each cluster after the average depth of its stations. depth_order <- clustered |> summarise(depth = mean(depth_m), .by = .cluster) |> arrange(depth) |> mutate(group = c("Shallow", "Mid-depth", "Deep")) clustered <- clustered |> left_join(select(depth_order, .cluster, group), by = ".cluster") |> mutate(group = factor(group, levels = depth_order$group)) clustered |> summarise(stations = n(), `species present` = round(mean(present == "yes"), 2), `mean abundance` = round(mean(abundance), 2), .by = group) |> arrange(group) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|group | stations| species present| mean abundance| |:---------|--------:|---------------:|--------------:| |Shallow | 239| 0.81| 4.97| |Mid-depth | 298| 0.82| 4.24| |Deep | 263| 0.69| 2.52|
::: ::: The species turns up at about four in five shallow and mid-depth stations, and at 69% of deep ones, where the average catch is half that of the shallow group (@fig-clusters). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_space <- ggplot(clustered, aes(depth_m, temperature_c, colour = group)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL, title = "The groups k-means found") p_abund <- ggplot(clustered, aes(group, abundance, fill = group)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) + guides(fill = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Abundance", title = "Abundance, never shown to it") p_space + p_abund + plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: stations by depth and temperature, coloured by the group k-means assigned. Right: abundance in each group. The clustering never saw abundance, yet the shallow group holds about twice as many animals as the deep one.](types-of-learning_files/figure-html/fig-clusters-1.png){#fig-clusters fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a scatter plot of temperature against depth, with points coloured into three groups that mostly follow depth, with some overlap: shallow and warm on the left, mid-depth in the middle, deep and cold on the right. The right panel is a boxplot of abundance for each group; the shallow group has the highest median and the deep group the lowest.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Supervised | Unsupervised | | --- | --- | --- | | Needs | An answer for every training station | Only the measurements | | Returns | A prediction of the answer | A group, with no meaning attached | | Can be checked | Against stations held back, whose answers are known | Only indirectly, against things it never saw | | Example here | The chance of presence | Shallow, mid-depth and deep groups | So the groups do differ in the species, although k-means never saw a single catch. This is unsupervised learning at its most useful and its most tempting. Ask for six groups and you get six, each just as confidently defined. [Section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) covers the checks that tell a real structure from an artefact of the method. ## Limits of these divisions **Generative models depend on their description of the data.** A bell curve suited the stations with the species and misdescribed those without it. A discriminative model makes fewer assumptions about the data, which is one reason it is the usual default. **Unsupervised does not mean assumption-free.** Choosing k-means, choosing three groups, choosing the variables and their scaling: each is a modelling decision, and each shapes the groups. **Labels are often less solid than they look.** Two specialists classifying the same seabed images disagree more often than most people expect. A supervised model can never be more reliable than the labels it learned from. **The boundaries blur in practice.** Semi-supervised learning combines a few labels with many unlabelled examples; self-supervised learning builds labels from the data's own structure. The divisions on this page are a teaching map, not a law. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - A discriminative model learns the answer: the chance of an outcome at each value of the predictors. A generative model learns the data themselves, and can generate new examples. - Supervised learning needs examples with known answers. Regression predicts a quantity, classification a category. - Unsupervised learning has no answers. Methods such as k-means find groups, and will always return as many as you ask for. - Reinforcement learning learns from the consequences of actions, and is outside this course. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the clustering with `num_clusters = 6`, then with `num_clusters = 2`. Do the groups still look like real habitats? Which evidence would make you prefer one answer over another? 2. Replace temperature with depth in both presence models. Do the discriminative and generative curves still agree where most stations lie?
